newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Orthodox church says pope should not visit Russia.
newsitem.headline: Orthodox church says pope should not visit Russia.

text.p: It is still too early for Pope John Paul to visit Russia, although the Catholic church is coming round to Moscow's view that it should not encroach on Orthodox territory, church representatives said on Thursday.

"We...consider that a visit by the Pope today within the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) is not appropriate," said a senior church figure, Metropolitan Kiril of Smolensk and Kaliningrad.

"Such visits should end a hard and dark period, opening a new, bright page. It is important that they do not take on a promotional character but are aimed at resolving existing problems," he told the Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily.
A spokesman for the patriarch's office in Moscow backed the statement by Kiril, one of 17 Metropolitans in the Russian Orthodox church who rank just below its head, Patriarch Alexiy.
"The question of a meeting (between the Pope and the Patriarch) is being discussed but not here," he said by telephone.

"It should not be an advertising campaign for the Pope, but should symbolise true friendship and cooperation on this territory. But for this we need to overcome existing difficulties and conflicts," he said.

The Polish-born Pope, who played a key role in the collapse of communism in his homeland, has long wanted to visit Russia but religious sources say a trip would be unlikely without the support of the Russian Orthodox Church.
The Vatican announced a possible meeting with Alexiy in Hungary in July but later said Russian Orthodox churchmen had made it clear they felt the time was not ripe.
Tensions persist between the two denominations following the demise of the Soviet Union, which sparked a race to fill the spiritual vaccuum created by communism.

They stem in part from disputes over property confiscated from the Catholic Church and passed to the Russian Orthodox Church under communist rule in Russia and other former Soviet republics, including Ukraine, which are now in the CIS.
In Ukraine, where different branches of the Orthodox church are competing with each other as well as with a strong Greek Catholic church, relations are particularly tense.

A top Ukrainian Catholic cleric said in October he hoped tensions between the five million Catholics and 35 million Orthodox believers would ease sufficiently to allow the Pope, 76, to visit late next year.
But Kiril seemed unsure. "In Western Ukraine, if there's not open warfare, then the confrontation is unusually acute," he told the newspaper.
The patriarch's spokesman hinted that the Catholic church's attempt to spread in Russia -- where the Orthodox church is enjoying a revival of influence -- was also interfering with relations.
"Our position is, and Rome is beginning to agree with us, that the spread of the Catholic church in Russia should correspond to the needs of the Catholic congregation," he said.
He said the Catholic church was needed in places where Catholics from Germany, the Baltic states and so forth, lived.

"But only within these limits. Not in the places where Catholic parishes never existed, or no longer exist, that is on traditionally Orthodox territory," he said. In Moscow, that meant two Catholic churches were enough, he said.
